title: Reading John

objectives.can: Read a chapter of John with reduced help and describe what makes John's Greek plain: short clauses, a small vocabulary, καί and asyndeton.

explanation.summary: The Gospel of John is often the first whole book a learner reads, because its sentences are short and its words recur. This lesson describes what makes the Greek of John plain, and then sends you into a stretch of the book to read it.

sections.heading: Short clauses side by side
body: Grammarians describe John's sentences as built mostly from short clauses set next to each other, often joined by καί, and not from long chains of subordinate clauses. This is called parataxis. John 1:1 is a good specimen: three clauses, each with ἦν, each joined to the last by καί.
Each clause is complete by itself, so you can read John clause by clause: find the verb, find its subject, and move on. The skill is the one you practised in Stage 5, but with less to untangle.

sections.heading: A small, repeated vocabulary
body: John is often said to use a limited stock of words and to repeat them, so that a word met once returns within a few verses. In John 15 the verb μένω, 'I remain, stay', and the noun ἀγάπη, 'love', come back again and again; so do the verb ἀγαπάω and the noun ἐντολή, 'commandment'. Other words that readers associate with John are φῶς, ζωή, κόσμος, ἀλήθεια, μαρτυρέω and πιστεύω.

Repetition is part of how the book argues. When you meet a word a second time, check whether it means exactly what it meant before; John sometimes plays on a word, but just as often he simply says the same thing again.

sections.heading: Connectives, and the lack of them
body: Besides καί, John uses δέ, γάρ and especially οὖν. In narrative οὖν is very common: ὁ οὖν Ἰησοῦς in John 4:6. Grammarians point out that in John it is often a weak 'so' or 'then' that moves the story on, and not always a strong 'therefore'.

John also leaves connectives out. A sentence with no connecting word at all is called asyndeton. John 11:35 is the best known: ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, three words, with nothing joining it to the sentence before. Asyndeton is common in John's speeches and in his narrative, and you will notice it as a sentence that begins directly with a verb or a subject.

sections.heading: Tenses and set phrases
body: Narrative in John often uses the present tense for past events: ἔρχεται and λέγει in John 4:7. Grammarians call this the historical present. You translate it by its context, usually with an English past tense; Greek does not mean that the event is happening now.

The speeches of Jesus in John use the pattern ἐγώ εἰμι followed by a predicate: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος in John 15:1 and 15:5. They also use ἵνα very freely, sometimes for purpose and sometimes to say what a commandment or a thing consists in: ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ ἐμὴ ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους in 15:12.
Another habit is to place a noun phrase first and then pick it up with a pronoun: ὁ μένων ἐν ἐμοί … οὗτος φέρει καρπόν in 15:5, 'the one who remains in me … this one bears fruit'.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read John 15:1–11 once for the plan. The vine and the branches give the images, μένω gives the rhythm, and ἐάν with the subjunctive gives the conditions. Then read again, clause by clause, looking up only the words you do not know. The questions test what a clause says and how its parts relate, not your memory of vocabulary.

misunderstandings: Plain does not mean shallow, and short clauses do not make every sentence easy. Check which noun a pronoun like οὗτος or αὐτός points back to, and which verb has which subject.
οὖν is not always 'therefore'. In narrative it is often just 'so' or 'then'. Decide from the context.
A historical present such as λέγει is not a statement about now. Read it as part of the story.
ἵνα is not always 'in order that'. After a noun like ἐντολή it often says what the commandment is, as in John 15:12.

deeper.heading: Why John seems unlike the other Gospels
body: Readers have long noticed that John's Greek is simple in its grammar but unlike Matthew, Mark and Luke in its rhythm: long speeches, repeated words, few of the quick narrative links of Mark. Scholars give different explanations, including the influence of Semitic speech patterns and the author's own manner. The grammar can describe the habits; it cannot decide between the explanations.

examples.analysis: Three clauses of the same shape. Each has ἦν, and καί joins each clause to the next: a clear case of short clauses side by side. Note that ἦν is imperfect, 'was', and that each clause could stand as a sentence on its own.

examples.analysis: ὁ οὖν Ἰησοῦς: οὖν stands in second place in the clause, as particles usually do, and here moves the story on from the setting of the well to Jesus sitting down. It is best read as 'so' or 'then'. ἐκαθέζετο is imperfect, 'he was sitting'.

examples.analysis: ἔρχεται and λέγει are both present tense, but the scene is in the past: a historical present. There is no connective between the two sentences, so this verse also shows asyndeton. The speech that follows, Δός μοι πεῖν, is a short imperative with an infinitive.

examples.analysis: ἐδάκρυσεν is aorist active indicative, third person singular, and ὁ Ἰησοῦς is its subject. The whole sentence is the verb and its subject, with nothing to link it to the sentence before: asyndeton, here giving the sentence great weight.

options: A purpose clause: in order that you remain
A question: do you remain in me?
A condition: if you remain in me

options: I loved the Father, and you loved me
The Father loved me, and I too loved you
The Father loved you, and you loved me

options: By καί, side by side, with no subordinate clause
They are not joined; each has asyndeton
By ἵνα, each clause giving the purpose of the last
By ὅτι, each clause giving the reason for the last
check.explain: καί stands before the second and third clauses. This simple coordination is the paratactic style described above.

reading.why: Eleven verses where μένω and ἀγάπη recur, clauses are short, ἐάν-conditions follow one another, and ἐγώ εἰμι opens the speech.
